questions.topic: Iceberg and Delta: Metadata Layers That Add ACID to Object Storage
questions.question: What do open table formats add above object-store data files?
options: A transactional metadata layer that defines the committed table state
A block device driver that lets engines edit object bytes in place
A requirement that every table be stored in a row-oriented file format
A separate storage bucket that holds one directory for each query

questions.topic: Iceberg and Delta: Metadata Layers That Add ACID to Object Storage
questions.question: Why do readers consult table metadata instead of listing a data prefix?
options: Because metadata stores the row values themselves, so no scan is needed
Because metadata names the exact file set committed by a snapshot
Because a prefix listing cannot return keys once a bucket is versioned
Because data files carry no schema, so a listing cannot be interpreted

questions.topic: Iceberg and Delta: Metadata Layers That Add ACID to Object Storage
questions.question: What should happen when two writers rewrite the same files from one parent snapshot?
options: Both commits should succeed, since each wrote its own immutable files
The later writer should delete the earlier snapshot and its metadata
Conflict validation should reject the second, incompatible commit
Readers should merge both file sets and deduplicate the rows later

questions.topic: Iceberg and Delta: Metadata Layers That Add ACID to Object Storage
questions.question: What operational requirement remains after a table metadata commit?
options: The referenced data objects may be deleted once the commit is durable
Readers must list every prefix to confirm the snapshot is complete
Retention policies become unnecessary because snapshots are immutable
Every referenced object must stay readable, durable and safe from cleanup

questions.topic: Iceberg and Delta: Metadata Layers That Add ACID to Object Storage
questions.question: Why does updating two formatted tables separately not create one atomic dataset transaction?
options: Each table commits on its own boundary, so versions can be mismatched
Open formats forbid more than one table inside a single storage bucket
Object stores reject manifests that reference more than one table name
The two tables must share an identical schema before any commit lands

questions.topic: Iceberg and Delta: Metadata Layers That Add ACID to Object Storage
questions.question: Why must engine compatibility be tested even when a feature exists in a format specification?
options: Because a specification defines file layout but carries no semantics
Because reader and writer implementations support features unevenly
Because each engine keeps its own private copy of the object store
Because a metadata commit makes the software version irrelevant

questions.topic: Snapshots and Time Travel
questions.question: What is a table snapshot?
options: A mutable working copy of one data file kept beside the original
A cache of query results attached to the table for faster reads
An immutable description of the table's state at a single commit
A listing of every prefix the table's bucket currently contains

questions.topic: Snapshots and Time Travel
questions.question: What is a key use of time travel?
options: Editing objects from an earlier snapshot without rewriting them
Removing lineage records so a table's history stays compact
Disabling rollback so the newest commit is always authoritative
Reproducing or auditing the table exactly as it stood earlier

questions.topic: Snapshots and Time Travel
questions.question: Why is snapshot ID more deterministic than a timestamp for lineage?
options: It names one exact committed state, free of clock and ordering doubt
It equals the row count at commit, so a mismatch is easy to detect
It replaces the parent reference, so the chain cannot be walked back
It encodes each data value, so the state can be rebuilt from the ID

questions.topic: Snapshots and Time Travel
questions.question: Why is time travel not automatically a permanent backup?
options: Because snapshots record only counts and never reference data files
Because expiration and cleanup can remove old metadata and files
Because each snapshot can be read once before it is marked consumed
Because reading an old snapshot rewrites the rows it was built from

questions.topic: Snapshots and Time Travel
questions.question: A six-hour query is pinned to a snapshot. What must retention guarantee?
options: That the snapshot expires as soon as a newer commit lands on the table
That only the newest data file of each partition is kept in the bucket
That its referenced files outlive the query and a safety margin
That the query is rebased onto the current snapshot every hour

questions.topic: Snapshots and Time Travel
questions.question: What is a risk of forgotten branches or protected tags?
options: They cannot reference a snapshot once the main branch advances
They delete data from the main branch when their retention expires
They force every later schema change to narrow a column's type
They pin sensitive or costly history so cleanup never reclaims it

questions.topic: Schema Evolution Rules: Safe vs Breaking Changes
questions.question: Which schema change is usually safest?
options: Adding a nullable column that old files simply read back as a null value
Narrowing a large integer column to a smaller integer width
Reusing a dropped field ID for a newly introduced column
Redefining a timestamp column's timezone after historical data landed

questions.topic: Schema Evolution Rules: Safe vs Breaking Changes
questions.question: Why do stable field IDs matter?
options: They let a reader compress every column with one dictionary per table
They keep a column's identity constant across renames and old files
They fix the partition size so each file holds the same row count
They remove the need for contracts between producers and consumers

questions.topic: Schema Evolution Rules: Safe vs Breaking Changes
questions.question: Why is adding a required column without a historical value breaking?
options: Because a required column cannot be given a name that old files lack
Because every old file must be rewritten to make room for the field
Because historical rows cannot satisfy the new not-null invariant
Because every query is then forced to reference the new column

questions.topic: Schema Evolution Rules: Safe vs Breaking Changes
questions.question: What is the safest migration sequence for replacing a field?
options: Drop the old field, then tell consumers to adopt the replacement
Reuse the old field's ID so existing readers need no configuration change
Rewrite one representative file and let the rest migrate lazily
Add the new field, dual write, backfill, migrate readers, then drop

questions.topic: Schema Evolution Rules: Safe vs Breaking Changes
questions.question: Why can an engine-allowed timestamp type change still be unsafe?
options: The timezone or precision meaning of the stored values can shift
Parquet has no timestamp type, so the cast writes a string column
Schema evolution discards the clock used to order table commits
Field IDs are recomputed, so old files map onto the row counter

questions.topic: Schema Evolution Rules: Safe vs Breaking Changes
questions.question: Why should a dropped field ID never be reused?
options: Because identifiers grow too long once a table has many columns
Because old files would surface under the new column's meaning
Because reusing an ID blocks any later addition of nullable columns
Because the table's storage region is derived from its field IDs

questions.topic: Safe Backfills on Immutable Snapshots
questions.question: How should a safe backfill publish rewritten history?
options: By editing the active data files partition by partition as it runs
By expiring the old snapshots first so readers cannot mix versions
By writing immutable replacements, validating them, then committing once
By exposing the staging prefix so readers pick up files as they land

questions.topic: Safe Backfills on Immutable Snapshots
questions.question: Why pin the backfill's input snapshot?
options: To stop validation from comparing the old and the proposed snapshots
To halt every upstream producer for the duration of the rewrite
To make reruns non-deterministic so duplicates are easy to spot
To keep a long job from reading a moving mixture of source states

questions.topic: Safe Backfills on Immutable Snapshots
questions.question: How should a failed pre-commit backfill output be classified?
options: As unreferenced orphan objects rather than as active table state
As current table data that readers will find on the next listing
As the authoritative replacement for every partition it touched
As a retained snapshot that time travel must be able to resolve

questions.topic: Safe Backfills on Immutable Snapshots
questions.question: Why compare business measures as well as row counts?
options: Because a matching row count proves each value was transformed right
Because equal row counts can still hide values transformed incorrectly
Because business measures decide which object keys the writer uses
Because a backfill can never change a column's null rate by design

questions.topic: Safe Backfills on Immutable Snapshots
questions.question: Another writer updates a partition in the backfill scope after planning. What should the commit do?
options: Overwrite the newer files, since the backfill planned that scope first
Delete both generations and let the next scheduled run rebuild them
Detect the conflict and rebase or retry against the newer snapshot
Commit both file sets and let a later compaction drop the duplicates

questions.topic: Safe Backfills on Immutable Snapshots
questions.question: How can a huge multi-commit backfill avoid exposing mixed logic to consumers?
options: Emit no version marker, so consumers cannot tell the generations apart
Point consumers at the staging prefix and let them filter partial data
Expire the previous snapshot while the new partitions are still landing
Publish a dataset generation or view pointer once every part is ready

questions.topic: Index Rebuild-and-Swap: The Atomic Alias Mechanism
questions.question: What is the purpose of a stable search-index alias?
options: To point one logical name at the physical index now serving traffic
To store the document bodies apart from the index that scores them
To rewrite source identifiers so every generation shares a key space
To block validation queries from reaching a newly built index

questions.topic: Index Rebuild-and-Swap: The Atomic Alias Mechanism
questions.question: Why build a new index beside the serving index?
options: So rollback becomes impossible once the new generation is validated
So a complete generation can be validated before anything is exposed
So existing vectors can be modified in place while queries continue
So the corpus never has to be pinned to a single point in time

questions.topic: Index Rebuild-and-Swap: The Atomic Alias Mechanism
questions.question: What problem arises if only the read alias switches while writers still target the old index?
options: The new index inherits duplicate aliases that resolve unpredictably later
All read traffic stops until the write alias is moved to match it
The generations diverge, since new writes never reach the served index
The pinned corpus snapshot advances on its own to include new writes

questions.topic: Index Rebuild-and-Swap: The Atomic Alias Mechanism
questions.question: Why should cache keys include index generation or scoring version?
options: Because a cache cannot store the query text alongside its results
Because an alias never changes once the first generation has been built
Because physical indexes carry no name that a cache key could use
Because results scored by the old generation would otherwise survive

questions.topic: Index Rebuild-and-Swap: The Atomic Alias Mechanism
questions.question: Which process gives the strongest cutover correctness?
options: Pin the corpus, build, validate, catch up writes, then switch routing
Write each document to both indexes in a random order, then switch
Delete the old index first so validation cannot read stale documents
Switch the alias as soon as the first shard reports that it is ready

questions.topic: Index Rebuild-and-Swap: The Atomic Alias Mechanism
questions.question: Why retain the previous physical index after alias swap?
options: Because it must keep receiving every write until the next rebuild
Because rollback is then a pointer move while guardrails are watched
Because the alias is required to resolve to both generations at once
Because a newly built index cannot be deleted while an alias exists
